prompt.context_jp: 朱雀の朗々とした声＿＿営業部の午後に響き、鶸田は肩をすぼめて先輩の話に耳を傾けた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 朱雀の朗々とした声＿＿営業部の午後に響き…
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle introduces Suzaku's voice as new sensory information in the scene?

feedback.correct_en: The sentence opens the chapter by having Suzaku's voice suddenly fill the room — a brand-new perceptual event. が marks that newly-introduced subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat the voice as an already-established topic, which doesn't fit a scene-opening description. を doesn't work because 響く is intransitive.

contrast_examples.jp: 声が響いた。
contrast_examples.en: A voice rang out. (new event)

contrast_examples.jp: その声は低かった。
contrast_examples.en: That voice was low. (voice already in discourse)

prompt.context_jp: 怒られること＿＿極端に苦手な鶸田にとって、この講義は救いにも呪いにも聞こえる。
prompt.prompt_jp: 怒られること＿＿極端に苦手な鶸田…
prompt.prompt_en: Inside the relative clause describing Hiwada, which particle marks what he is bad at?

feedback.correct_en: With 苦手 (and similar predicates like 好き・嫌い), the thing you're bad at is marked with が. In a relative clause, は can't appear anyway.
feedback.incorrect_en: は is almost never used inside a relative clause like this one. に doesn't pair with 苦手 as its object.

contrast_examples.jp: 数学が苦手だ。
contrast_examples.en: I'm bad at math.

contrast_examples.jp: 怒られるのが怖い人。
contrast_examples.en: A person who is afraid of being scolded.

prompt.context_jp: 朱雀の話＿＿一区切りつくと、鷹野はふうと呼吸を整え…
prompt.prompt_jp: 朱雀の話＿＿一区切りつくと…
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the subject inside this 〜と time clause?

feedback.correct_en: Subordinate clauses ending in 〜と typically take が for their internal subject because the clause is a self-contained event, not a topic comment.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would try to make 朱雀の話 the sentence-level topic, but here the main clause is about Takano's reaction. に doesn't fit the intransitive 一区切りつく.

contrast_examples.jp: 雨がやむと、鳥が鳴き出した。
contrast_examples.en: When the rain stopped, the birds began to sing.

contrast_examples.jp: 雨はもうやんだ。
contrast_examples.en: The rain has already stopped. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: 朱雀の目にも、感嘆と嫉妬＿＿半分ずつ滲んでいた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 感嘆と嫉妬＿＿半分ずつ滲んでいた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks what appeared in Suzaku's eyes?

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is describing a freshly observed, concrete sight — admiration and jealousy showing up in his eyes. New-information が fits this descriptive, perceptual reading.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame these emotions as pre-established topics being commented on, which clashes with the vivid 'half-and-half seeping' image. を doesn't fit the intransitive 滲む.

contrast_examples.jp: 目に涙が浮かんだ。
contrast_examples.en: Tears welled up in his eyes.

contrast_examples.jp: 涙はすぐに乾いた。
contrast_examples.en: The tears quickly dried. (already in discourse)

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田＿＿自分の膝が細かく震え出したことに気づき、逃げ場のなさに首まで熱くなった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鶸田＿＿自分の膝が細かく震え出したことに気づき…
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks Hiwada, the ongoing viewpoint character of this scene?

feedback.correct_en: Hiwada is the established topic of this whole scene; the sentence is a comment about him. は signals topic continuation. Note the embedded 膝が震え出した uses が for the newly-observed subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would re-introduce Hiwada as new information, which clashes with him being the viewpoint character throughout. で doesn't fit a human experiencer here.

contrast_examples.jp: 鶸田は震えに気づいた。
contrast_examples.en: Hiwada noticed the trembling. (topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 鶸田が最初に気づいた。
contrast_examples.en: It was Hiwada who noticed first. (identification)

prompt.context_jp: 温和な人ほど、いざ怒らせると底が知れないという事実を、鶸田＿＿身をもって刻み込んだ気がした。
prompt.prompt_jp: …事実を、鶸田＿＿身をもって刻み込んだ気がした。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks Hiwada as the topic of this reflective sentence?

feedback.correct_en: Hiwada is the ongoing topic/experiencer; the sentence delivers his personal takeaway. は keeps him as the stable topic across this reflective comment.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would single him out as if contrasting with someone else who didn't learn it, which isn't the point. に doesn't work as the subject marker here.

contrast_examples.jp: 鶸田は深く反省した。
contrast_examples.en: Hiwada reflected deeply. (topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 鶸田がそれを言った。
contrast_examples.en: It was Hiwada who said that. (identification)

prompt.context_jp: 事の起こり＿＿鷹野が担当したECサイトの誤字だと、道すがら鳩山が何度も確認していた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 事の起こり＿＿鷹野が担当したECサイトの誤字だと…
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks '事の起こり' here?

feedback.correct_en: '事の起こりは〜だ' is a classic topic-comment frame: 'As for how it started, it was…'. は sets up the topic that the rest of the sentence defines.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make the clause an identification ('it is the origin that…'), which doesn't fit the explanatory tone. を doesn't fit the copular predicate.

contrast_examples.jp: 原因はミスだった。
contrast_examples.en: The cause was a mistake. (topic-comment)

contrast_examples.jp: 原因がやっと分かった。
contrast_examples.en: The cause finally became clear. (new information)

prompt.context_jp: 頭を下げれば下げるほど、社長の言葉＿＿容赦なく降り注いだ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 社長の言葉＿＿容赦なく降り注いだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the president's words in this narrative comment?

feedback.correct_en: The president and her tirade are already established in the scene; the sentence makes a generalizing comment ('the more he bowed, the more mercilessly her words fell'). は fits that topical, summarizing voice.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it feel like a sudden, first-time observation, which doesn't match the ongoing cumulative tone. で doesn't fit the intransitive 降り注ぐ.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の声はますます大きくなった。
contrast_examples.en: His voice grew louder and louder. (ongoing topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 突然、怒鳴り声が響いた。
contrast_examples.en: Suddenly a shout rang out. (new event)

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野の一撃で、応接間の空気＿＿凍りついた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 応接間の空気＿＿凍りついた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits this dramatic, scene-shifting beat?

feedback.correct_en: This is a single sudden event — the air freezing the instant Takano strikes. New-event が captures that punch. The 空気 isn't a pre-set topic; it's what suddenly changes.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn it into a general statement about the air, losing the sudden-change impact. に doesn't mark a subject.

contrast_examples.jp: 部屋の空気が一変した。
contrast_examples.en: The air in the room completely changed. (sudden event)

contrast_examples.jp: 部屋の空気はいつも重い。
contrast_examples.en: The air in this room is always heavy. (habitual topic)

prompt.context_jp: 畳みかける鷹野の言葉に、社長の顔から血の気＿＿引いていく。
prompt.prompt_jp: 社長の顔から血の気＿＿引いていく。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks '血の気' in this descriptive moment?

feedback.correct_en: '血の気が引く' is a fixed descriptive expression — the blood draining is a newly observed physical reaction. が is the standard particle in this idiom.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would isolate 血の気 as a contrast topic, which breaks the idiom. を doesn't fit the intransitive 引く here.

contrast_examples.jp: 顔から血の気が引いた。
contrast_examples.en: The blood drained from his face. (idiomatic)

contrast_examples.jp: 顔色が悪い。
contrast_examples.en: He looks pale.

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田＿＿自分の中の熱がゆっくりと引いていくのを感じる。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鶸田＿＿自分の中の熱がゆっくりと引いていくのを感じる。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks Hiwada, the viewpoint character?

feedback.correct_en: Hiwada remains the sentence-level topic; the embedded 熱が引く uses が for the newly-observed internal change. The は/が pair here is a textbook topic–new-info split.
feedback.incorrect_en: が for 鶸田 would duel with the embedded が and reduce him to just one of several new subjects. に doesn't mark a sentient experiencer here.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は心が落ち着くのを感じた。
contrast_examples.en: He felt his heart calm down.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が最初に気づいた。
contrast_examples.en: It was he who noticed first.

prompt.context_jp: 社長の言葉＿＿、なぜか自分の胸にもいちばん深く残っていたからだ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 社長の言葉＿＿、なぜか自分の胸にも…残っていた…
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the president's words here?

feedback.correct_en: This is a reason clause (〜からだ) explaining why Hatoyama went home early. Reason clauses typically take が for the subject that caused the state. The 言葉 are singled out as the specific thing lingering.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would try to topicalize the words at the sentence level, but Hatoyama is the implicit topic — the words are new, identifying information. を doesn't fit intransitive 残る.

contrast_examples.jp: その言葉が心に残った。
contrast_examples.en: Those words stayed in my heart.

contrast_examples.jp: その言葉は忘れた。
contrast_examples.en: I forgot those words. (contrastive topic)

prompt.context_jp: 妻の目に＿＿まだ怪訝そうな色が残っていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 妻の目に＿＿まだ怪訝そうな色が残っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle, attached after に, best captures the implicit contrast ('elsewhere maybe not, but in her eyes…')?

feedback.correct_en: The に+は combination contrasts her eyes with the rest of the resolved mood: his words soothed things, but in her eyes doubt still lingered. は after a case particle flags that contrast.
feedback.incorrect_en: が can't follow に in this slot. を doesn't fit either — 残る is intransitive and 色 is already the subject (marked by が later in the sentence).

contrast_examples.jp: 顔には笑みが戻ったが、目には不安が残っていた。
contrast_examples.en: A smile returned to his face, but worry lingered in his eyes.

contrast_examples.jp: 目に涙が浮かんだ。
contrast_examples.en: Tears came to his eyes. (no contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 恋愛の話になると、皆＿＿一段、口が軽くなる。
prompt.prompt_jp: 恋愛の話になると、皆＿＿一段、口が軽くなる。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks '皆' inside this generalizing conditional sentence?

feedback.correct_en: In 〜と conditional clauses describing a general pattern, the subject of the result is typically marked with が. The sentence states a tendency: whenever love talk starts, everyone loosens up.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would try to make 皆 a topic in a subordinate clause, which は generally avoids. に doesn't fit a human subject here.

contrast_examples.jp: 春になると、花が咲く。
contrast_examples.en: When spring comes, flowers bloom.

contrast_examples.jp: 皆はもう帰った。
contrast_examples.en: Everyone has already gone home. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野の顔から、ふだんの澄ました表情＿＿すっと消えた。
prompt.prompt_jp: ふだんの澄ました表情＿＿すっと消えた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits this abrupt change on Takano's face?

feedback.correct_en: This describes a sudden visible change — the composed look vanishing in an instant. New-event が carries that observational, cinematic feel.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn it into a generalization ('as for her usual composure, it disappeared'), losing the suddenness. を doesn't fit the intransitive 消える.

contrast_examples.jp: 笑顔がすっと消えた。
contrast_examples.en: The smile vanished in an instant.

contrast_examples.jp: 笑顔はもう戻らなかった。
contrast_examples.en: The smile never came back. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: 「とにかく “怒られ道”は＿＿が深い 適切な謝り方をクリエートするんだ」
prompt.prompt_jp: “怒られ道”は＿＿が深い
prompt.prompt_en: Which word fits the fixed phrase '〜が深い' meaning 'profound'?

feedback.correct_en: 奥が深い is the set collocation for 'profound / has hidden depths'. Suzaku is dramatically framing the art of being scolded as a deep discipline.
feedback.incorrect_en: 中が深い doesn't exist as a collocation. 底が深い is possible but implies 'bottomless/unfathomable' in a darker, often negative sense, not 'rich and worth mastering'.

contrast_examples.jp: 日本語は奥が深い。
contrast_examples.en: Japanese is a deep language.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の闇は底が知れない。
contrast_examples.en: The depth of his darkness is unfathomable.

prompt.context_jp: 「基本は3つ “＿＿は絶対にしない” “相手の話の腰は折らない”…」
prompt.prompt_jp: “＿＿は絶対にしない”
prompt.prompt_en: Suzaku's first rule of apologizing. What are you not supposed to do?

feedback.correct_en: 言い訳をする/しない ('make/don't make excuses') is the standard collocation. In an apology, offering excuses is the classic no-no Suzaku warns against.
feedback.incorrect_en: 言い回し means 'phrasing' and doesn't pair with しない. 物言い means 'manner of speaking' or 'objection' and doesn't fit the apology-rule framing.

contrast_examples.jp: 言い訳はいいから謝れ。
contrast_examples.en: Enough excuses — apologize.

contrast_examples.jp: 丁寧な言い回しを選ぶ。
contrast_examples.en: Choose a polite phrasing.

prompt.context_jp: 「“相手の話の＿＿は折らない”」
prompt.prompt_jp: 相手の話の＿＿は折らない
prompt.prompt_en: Which word completes this idiom meaning 'don't interrupt'?

feedback.correct_en: 話の腰を折る ('to break the waist of a conversation') is the set idiom for interrupting or derailing someone's story. The body part is fixed as 腰.
feedback.incorrect_en: 首を折る or 肩を折る aren't idiomatic in this sense. Swapping body parts breaks the fixed expression.

contrast_examples.jp: 話の腰を折って悪いけど…
contrast_examples.en: Sorry to interrupt, but…

contrast_examples.jp: 話の途中で割り込む。
contrast_examples.en: To cut in mid-conversation. (plain phrasing)

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田は＿＿をもって刻み込んだ気がした。
prompt.prompt_jp: ＿＿をもって刻み込んだ
prompt.prompt_en: Which word completes this idiom meaning 'through personal experience'?

feedback.correct_en: 身をもって is a fixed expression meaning 'with one's own body / through firsthand experience'. Hiwada just lived through Hatoyama's scary mock-anger, so he learned it the hard way.
feedback.incorrect_en: 心をもって exists but means 'with heart/sincerity' — not firsthand experience. 手をもって isn't a set phrase in this sense.

contrast_examples.jp: 身をもって体験する。
contrast_examples.en: To experience firsthand.

contrast_examples.jp: 心を込めて作る。
contrast_examples.en: To make something with heart.

prompt.context_jp: 「あっ とにかく ＿＿と言っては何ですが 次回のＥＣサイトの保守費用から 割り引きさせていただきますので…」
prompt.prompt_jp: ＿＿と言っては何ですが
prompt.prompt_en: Hatoyama is offering a discount as compensation. Which business noun fits here?

feedback.correct_en: おわびと言っては何ですが…('I hesitate to call it an apology, but…') is a standard polite set-up for offering compensation after an error. The context — a mistake they're trying to make up for — demands おわび.
feedback.incorrect_en: お礼 ('thanks') would make it sound like a reward, not an apology. お祝い ('congratulations') is wildly out of place here.

contrast_examples.jp: おわびと言っては何ですが、こちらを…
contrast_examples.en: I hesitate to call it an apology, but please accept this…

contrast_examples.jp: お礼と言っては何ですが、お受け取りください。
contrast_examples.en: I hesitate to call it a thank-you, but please accept this.

prompt.context_jp: 「確かに彼はミスをしました ですが 心から反省し ＿＿ 謝っています」
prompt.prompt_jp: 心から反省し ＿＿ 謝っています
prompt.prompt_en: Which four-character compound best fits Takano's defense of Hiwada?

feedback.correct_en: 誠心誠意 ('with utmost sincerity') is the standard business-speech idiom paired with 謝る. It emphasizes the sincerity of the apology Takano is defending.
feedback.incorrect_en: 一心不乱 means 'single-mindedly' and pairs with concentration, not apologies. 単刀直入 means 'straight to the point' and doesn't modify 謝る.

contrast_examples.jp: 誠心誠意、対応いたします。
contrast_examples.en: We will respond with utmost sincerity.

contrast_examples.jp: 一心不乱に勉強する。
contrast_examples.en: To study single-mindedly.

prompt.context_jp: 「＿＿です！」(鷹野の決め台詞、ドラマ「半沢」から)
prompt.prompt_jp: ＿＿です！
prompt.prompt_en: Takano's famous one-liner, borrowed from the Hanzawa Naoki drama.

feedback.correct_en: 倍返し ('paying back double') is the iconic Hanzawa Naoki catchphrase. The next sentence even confirms Takano watched the drama the day before.
feedback.incorrect_en: 恩返し means 'repaying kindness' — the opposite nuance. お返し is a neutral 'return gift/favor', not a retaliation.

contrast_examples.jp: やられたらやり返す。倍返しだ！
contrast_examples.en: If they hit us, we hit back — double!

contrast_examples.jp: 親に恩返しをしたい。
contrast_examples.en: I want to repay my parents' kindness.

prompt.context_jp: 「言葉が足りないから ＿＿が増すの」
prompt.prompt_jp: 言葉が足りないから ＿＿が増す
prompt.prompt_en: What grows when communication is lacking, according to the president?

feedback.correct_en: 不信感 ('distrust') is exactly what the president concludes grows when people hold back words — the lesson that then ripples into Hatoyama's home life.
feedback.incorrect_en: 達成感 ('sense of accomplishment') is positive — it wouldn't grow from lack of words. 緊張感 ('tension') is plausible but misses the specific trust theme the chapter builds around.

contrast_examples.jp: 説明不足で不信感が増す。
contrast_examples.en: Lack of explanation breeds distrust.

contrast_examples.jp: 成功して達成感を得る。
contrast_examples.en: Succeed and feel a sense of accomplishment.

prompt.context_jp: 鳩山が老舗の社長に向かって最初に発する一言。どちらが取引先の社長への謝罪としてより自然ですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural as Hatoyama's opening apology to the client's president?

choices.text: A: 社長… この度は 本当に すいませんでした
B: 社長… この度 めっちゃ ごめんなさいね

feedback.correct_en: A is the version in the story and matches the business-apology register: この度は + humble apology. Even すいません is informal for 申し訳ございません, but it still fits the apologetic team-leader tone.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's めっちゃ + ごめんなさいね is casual/feminine-casual speech — unthinkable when a sales team is apologizing to a long-established shop's president.

contrast_examples.jp: この度は申し訳ございませんでした。
contrast_examples.en: We are very sorry for the recent matter. (formal)

contrast_examples.jp: ごめんね、めっちゃ悪かった。
contrast_examples.en: Sorry, my bad. (casual, among friends)

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野が社長に反論を切り出す場面。どちらが自然ですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Takano is about to politely confront the president. Which opener sounds more natural?

choices.text: A: 大変 申し上げにくいんですが…
B: 大変 言いにくいんだけど…

feedback.correct_en: A uses the humble form 申し上げる + 〜にくいんですが, the standard cushioning phrase for softening pushback to a superior/client. This is exactly what's in the story.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses plain 言う + 〜んだけど, which is casual peer talk — far too flat for confronting an outside company's president.

contrast_examples.jp: 大変申し上げにくいのですが、ご確認をお願いできますか。
contrast_examples.en: I hesitate to bring this up, but could I ask you to check?

contrast_examples.jp: ちょっと言いにくいんだけど、さ…
contrast_examples.en: This is a bit hard to say, but, you know… (casual)

prompt.context_jp: 朱雀が後輩の鶸田に向かって説く場面。どちらが先輩から後輩へのくだけた口調として自然ですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural as Suzaku lecturing his junior Hiwada?

choices.text: A: いいか？ 鶸田 怒られの醍醐味は 許されたあとにある
B: よろしいでしょうか 鶸田様 怒られの醍醐味は 許された後にございます

feedback.correct_en: A matches the senpai-to-kōhai register: いいか？ as a casual attention-getter, plain-form 〜にある. It's the actual story line.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's 鶸田様 and ございます are over-polite keigo — a senior would never address a junior that way. The mismatch sounds sarcastic or absurd.

contrast_examples.jp: いいか、よく聞けよ。
contrast_examples.en: Listen up, okay? (senior to junior)

contrast_examples.jp: よろしいでしょうか、お客様。
contrast_examples.en: May I, sir/madam? (staff to customer)

prompt.context_jp: 鳩山が家に帰って、社長の言葉を妻に伝える場面。どちらが自然ですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Which version flows more naturally when Hatoyama echoes the president's words to his wife?

choices.text: A: 言葉が足りないから 不信感が増すんだ。だから… 何でも言い合える関係になろう
B: 不信感が増すんだ、言葉が足りないから。何でも言い合える関係になろう、だから

feedback.correct_en: A follows normal Japanese cause→effect ordering (〜から → result) and uses だから as a connector before the proposal. It's the story's actual phrasing and reads smoothly.
feedback.incorrect_en: B inverts clauses to a tacked-on afterthought style and ends with a dangling だから — grammatically possible as emphatic inversion in casual speech, but it sounds awkward and disorganized for a prepared heart-to-heart.

contrast_examples.jp: 疲れたから、休もう。
contrast_examples.en: I'm tired, so let's rest. (natural order)

contrast_examples.jp: 休もう、疲れたから。
contrast_examples.en: Let's rest — I'm tired. (emphatic inversion, more casual)

prompt.context_jp: 翌朝、鳩山が部長に心配をかけたお詫びを伝える場面。どちらが自然ですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Hatoyama is apologizing to the chief for worrying him. Which line sounds more natural?

choices.text: A: 部長 ご心配おかけしました 妻は不倫してませんでした
A: 部長 心配させてごめんね 妻 不倫してなかったわ

feedback.correct_en: A uses the humble ご心配おかけしました — the standard phrase to a superior — and 〜ませんでした. This is the story's phrasing and fits speaking to one's 部長 at work.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's 心配させてごめんね and 〜わ are casual, familiar speech appropriate to a close friend or spouse, not to one's department chief in the office.

contrast_examples.jp: ご心配おかけして申し訳ありません。
contrast_examples.en: I'm sorry for worrying you. (to a superior)

contrast_examples.jp: 心配させてごめんね。
contrast_examples.en: Sorry for making you worry. (to a close friend)
